title: God’s Battle Plan Was to Walk Around a City for Seven Days. Then the Walls Collapsed.
paragraphs: God’s Battle Plan Was to Walk Around a City for Seven Days. Then the Walls Collapsed.

Jericho looked impossible. God’s instructions looked unreasonable. Israel’s weapons were not enough. And before a single stone fell, God was teaching His people a truth we still struggle to believe: sometimes the wall in front of you is not merely something God intends to remove. Sometimes it is the place where He exposes what you actually trust.
There is something almost uncomfortable about the battle plan.
Walk.
That was part of it.
Not charge.
Not build siege ramps.
Not spend the night calculating where the defenses were weakest.
Walk around the city.
Then go back to camp.
Wake up the next day.
Walk around it again.
And again.
And again.
For six days.
Then, on the seventh day, circle Jericho seven times.
Priests would carry trumpets. The ark of the covenant would go with them. The people would remain under Joshua’s command concerning when to shout.
And after all of that strange obedience…
the walls would fall.
If you already know the story, familiarity can make it sound almost easy.
It was not.
Imagine being there.
You have crossed the Jordan. The promise is in front of you. But standing between you and the next step is a fortified city.
Jericho.
Joshua 6:1 describes the situation with striking Hebrew:
וִירִיחוֹ סֹגֶרֶת וּמְסֻגֶּרֶת
Vîrîḥô sōgeret ûmesuggeret.
The sense is that Jericho was tightly shut up—closed and secured.
The verse continues:
אֵין יוֹצֵא וְאֵין בָּא
’Ên yōṣē’ we’ên bā’.
“No one went out, and no one came in.”
Jericho was not casually waiting for Israel.
It was sealed.
Defensive.
Inaccessible.
And perhaps that is why this story still reaches into places we would rather keep hidden.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to stand in front of something that will not move.
You prayed.
Still there.
You cried.
Still there.
You tried to change.
Still there.
You promised God that this time would be different.
Still there.
The addiction still whispers.
The resentment still burns.
The shame still remembers your name.
The marriage still hurts.
The prodigal still has not come home.
The grief still wakes up before you do.
The temptation still knows where to find you.
The consequences of yesterday are still standing in the middle of today.
And somewhere inside your exhausted heart, you have begun asking the question faithful people sometimes feel guilty for asking:
“God… if You brought me this far, why is there still a wall?”
Then God speaks to Joshua.
And notice something astonishing.
The wall is still standing when God says:
רְאֵה נָתַתִּי בְיָדְךָ אֶת־יְרִיחוֹ
Re’eh, nātattî beyādekha ’et-Yerîḥô.

“See, I have given Jericho into your hand.”
—Joshua 6:2
Look carefully at the wording.
Jericho has not fallen yet.
Israel has not marched around it yet.
The trumpet has not sounded.
The people have not shouted.
Dust has not begun falling from the walls.
Yet God speaks of the victory as something He has given.
The Hebrew נָתַתִּי — nātattî comes from the verb natan, “to give.”
God does not begin by congratulating Israel on its military strength.
He begins with His gift.
That changes the center of the story.
Jericho is not primarily a monument to Israelite ingenuity.
It is a testimony to the God who keeps His word.
But here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
God promised the victory…
and then required Israel to obey Him while the wall still looked exactly like a wall.
That is where many of us struggle.
We want obedience after explanation.
God often calls us to obedience because He is trustworthy.
We want to understand the entire route before taking the next step.
God sometimes gives enough light for the next faithful step and asks us to trust Him with what we cannot yet see.

Israel was told to march around Jericho once each day for six days. Seven priests were to carry seven trumpets before the ark. On the seventh day, they were to circle the city seven times. Then, at Joshua’s command, the people were to shout.
Imagine the first day.
Footsteps.
Trumpets.
A fortified city towering above them.
Then they return to camp.
Nothing.
Second day.
Walk.
Return.
The wall is still there.
Third day.
Still there.
Fourth day.
Still there.
Fifth day.
Still there.
Sixth day.
Still standing.
Have you ever obeyed God and watched absolutely nothing seem to happen?
That can be one of the loneliest places in faith.
You forgave, but the wound still aches.
You stopped going back to the sin, but temptation did not stop coming back to you.
You opened your Bible again, but heaven did not suddenly feel close.
You started praying for your family, but they still seem far from Christ.
You chose integrity and lost an opportunity because of it.
You repented, but now you must live through consequences repentance does not instantly erase.
You have been walking…
and walking…
and walking…
and the wall has had the audacity to remain standing.
Maybe the miracle of Jericho did not begin when stones started falling.
Maybe, from the human side of the story, one of the first miracles was that Israel kept walking when the stones had not moved.
Faith is not pretending the wall is imaginary.
Biblical faith looks at the wall, hears the Word of God, and decides that the wall does not get the final word.
But Jericho must never be reduced to a motivational slogan.
This is not Scripture telling you to “manifest your breakthrough.”
It is not a divine formula promising that if you repeat something seven times, every financial problem, illness, relationship crisis, or personal dream will resolve exactly as you want.
Joshua 6 records a specific moment in God’s redemptive history, connected to His covenant purposes and His judgment upon Canaan.

The number seven is unmistakably repeated throughout the chapter—seven priests, seven trumpets, seven days, seven circuits on the seventh day—but the passage does not authorize Christians to turn seven into a magical technique.
The power was never in the number.
The power was never in Israel’s footsteps.
The power was never in the volume of their shout.
The power belonged to God.
And that matters because we are always tempted to turn gifts from God into formulas for controlling God.
“Maybe if I pray exactly like this…”
“Maybe if I give enough…”
“Maybe if I say the right words…”
“Maybe if I become spiritual enough…”
Then God will owe me my Jericho.
No.
Grace does not put God in our debt.
Faith does not manipulate Him.
God is God.
We are not.
And sometimes faithfulness ends with a wall collapsing.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like Paul pleading three times for the thorn to leave and hearing Christ say, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).
Sometimes faithfulness looks like Jesus in Gethsemane praying, “Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).
The Christian hope is not that God must make every earthly circumstance obey our preferred ending.
Our hope is that because of Jesus Christ, even suffering, waiting, weakness, persecution, loss, and death cannot separate God’s children from His love.
That is a much stronger Gospel than “God will give you whatever breakthrough you imagine.”
Then comes the seventh day.
They rise early.
Once around Jericho.
Twice.
Three times.
Four.
Five.
Six.
Imagine the exhaustion.
Imagine staring at the same stones you saw yesterday.
Then…
seven.
Joshua tells the people to shout.
The trumpets sound.
And Joshua 6:20 records:
וַתִּפֹּל הַחוֹמָה תַּחְתֶּיהָ
Vattippōl haḥômāh taḥtehā.
“And the wall fell down in its place,” commonly rendered along the sense of the wall falling down flat.
The wall that had announced, “You cannot enter,” was suddenly on the ground.
But if we stop there, we risk turning Jericho into nothing more than an inspirational victory story.
Joshua 6 is also a chapter of judgment.
That part should not be hidden because it makes modern readers uncomfortable.
The city was placed under חֵרֶם — ḥērem, a Hebrew term used in this context for something devoted to destruction under divine judgment.
This is difficult Scripture.
It should be treated with sobriety, not celebrated with bloodthirsty triumphalism.

According to the biblical storyline, Israel was not given a universal permission slip for religious violence. The conquest belongs to a particular covenantal and historical setting in which God acts as Judge. Deuteronomy had already made clear that Israel's possession of the land was not because Israel was inherently righteous (Deuteronomy 9:4–6), and the same covenant later warned Israel that persistent rebellion would bring judgment upon them too.
God is not tribal property.
He cannot be recruited to baptize our hatred.
Jericho should make us tremble before divine holiness as much as it makes us marvel at divine power.
And then, inside a city marked for judgment, Scripture gives us a scandal.
Rahab.
A woman with a past.
A Canaanite.
An outsider.
A woman Scripture identifies as a prostitute.
If human beings were writing a respectable religious story designed to impress respectable religious people, Rahab might have been edited out.
God did not edit her out.
Earlier, in Joshua 2, Rahab had hidden Israel’s spies and confessed what she had come to believe about Israel’s God:
“The LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.”
When Jericho fell, Rahab and those with her were spared according to the promise made to her.
Read that slowly.
Judgment was falling.
Walls were collapsing.
A city was being conquered.
And grace knew Rahab’s address.
That is where Jericho begins pointing beyond Jericho.
Because Rahab does not disappear after Joshua.
Her name appears again.
And again.
Then centuries later, Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
There, in the genealogy of the Messiah, stands a name some people might have preferred to hide.
Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 names her in the ancestry that leads to Jesus.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers her faith.
James 2:25 remembers the action that demonstrated it.
The woman who once lived inside the doomed city became part of the human family line through which the Messiah entered the world.
Tell me grace is not scandalous.
Her past did not become good.
Her sin did not become holy.
But her past was no longer powerful enough to cancel what God, in grace, was doing with her future.
That is the difference between biblical grace and cheap affirmation.
Jesus does not call darkness light.
He rescues sinners from darkness.
He does not rewrite our story by pretending our sin never mattered.
At the cross, He shows us exactly how much sin matters.
And then He shows us how much mercy costs.
Jericho had walls made of stone.
We build different kinds.
Pornography behind a locked screen.
Bitterness behind a smile.
Pride behind ministry.
Greed behind ambition.
Loneliness behind jokes.
Envy behind congratulations.
Lust behind secrecy.
Unforgiveness behind “I’m fine.”
Fear behind control.
Religious performance behind church attendance.
Some walls are built to keep other people out.
Others are built because we are terrified someone will discover what is inside.
And perhaps the most dangerous wall is the one we construct between our public Christianity and our private life.
People know the worship version of us.
God knows what happens when the music stops.
People see the verse we posted.
God sees the message we deleted.
People hear the testimony.
God remembers the compromise we are still protecting.
People call us strong.
God hears us crying at 2:13 in the morning.
And still…
He calls us.
Not into better hiding.
Into repentance.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside your carefully fortified life shouting, “Pretend harder.”
The Gospel is Christ calling sinners out of hiding.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance, carrying the sense of a change of mind that turns a person toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns.
It stops negotiating with the sin Jesus died to save us from.
It stops calling bondage “just who I am.”
It stops protecting what God is exposing.
It stops decorating the wall.
And it comes to Christ.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Not because you needed another article about an ancient city.
Because there is a wall in you.
Something you have been defending.
Something exhausting you.
Something nobody knows.
Something you keep promising to surrender “eventually.”
And perhaps the Holy Spirit has been putting His finger on it for longer than you want to admit.
Be careful here.
Do not turn Jericho into permission to name another person as “your wall” and imagine God exists to destroy everyone standing in your way.
Before asking God to bring down the walls around you, ask Him what must come down within you.
Your pride.
Your secret sin.
Your self-righteousness.
Your refusal to forgive.
Your need to control everything.
Your obsession with human approval.
Your belief that your worst chapter has made redemption impossible.
Because the deepest Christian victory is not getting everything we want.
It is belonging completely to Jesus.
And Jesus takes us somewhere even more astonishing than Jericho.
Jericho tells us about a city under judgment where one household receives mercy.
Calvary tells us about the sinless Son of God willingly bearing judgment so sinners could receive mercy.
At Jericho, a shout accompanied the fall of a wall.
At Calvary, Jesus cried out and gave up His spirit.
At Jericho, Rahab was brought out of a condemned city.
At Calvary, Christ opened the way for condemned sinners to be reconciled to God.
And on the third day, the stone meant to seal a grave could not imprison the risen King.
That is our center.
Not Jericho.
Jesus.
Not your breakthrough.
Jesus.
Not your success.
Jesus.
Not a better version of your old self.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people can become slightly better.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because the righteous Christ gave Himself for sinners.
Paul writes in Romans 5:8 that God demonstrates His love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
While.
We.
Were.
Still.
Sinners.
Rahab had a history.
Peter had a denial.
Paul had blood on his résumé.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace reached where human respectability could not.
This does not make sin small.
It makes the Savior magnificent.
Maybe you thought Christianity was about becoming clean enough for Jesus to tolerate you.
It is the opposite.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You repent.
You believe.
You entrust yourself to Christ.
You stop defending the ruins.
You stop hiding behind the wall.
You stop trying to become your own savior.
And you discover that the hands strong enough to judge sin are the hands that were pierced to save sinners.
That is why our theme will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing history.
Not by pretending your wounds never happened.
Not by renaming evil as good.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.

He rewrites everything by taking a story headed toward judgment and, through repentance and faith, bringing a sinner into grace, forgiveness, reconciliation, holiness, purpose, and ultimately resurrection life.
Look at Rahab.
Jericho was part of her biography.
It was not the final definition of her identity.
Maybe you need that sentence today.
Your worst chapter may be part of your biography.
It does not have to be the final definition of your identity.
Jesus still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still receives people who finally stop pretending they do not need Him.
Talk to God.
Confess it.
Name it.
Repent.
Ask Christ for mercy.
If you do not know what to pray, begin without impressive religious language.

“Jesus, have mercy on me. Forgive me. I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Turn my heart toward You. Teach me to follow You. I surrender what I have been hiding.”
Then do not confuse emotion with completion.
Take the next obedient step.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Turn away from the sin.
Make restitution where biblical wisdom requires it.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Become rooted in a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and Christ is exalted.
Keep walking.
Even when the wall still looks like a wall.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, be brave enough to say it.
Or tell your testimony.
Someone reading the comments may be standing where you once stood.
Your honesty may remind them that grace can reach their Jericho too.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help biblical encouragement reach more people. Christ cannot be bought, grace cannot be purchased, and salvation is not merchandise.

Your support helps us keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the message of Jesus before believers, seekers, struggling Christians, the spiritually exhausted, and people who may never walk through the doors of a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
Invite your family. Invite the friend whose faith is fading. Invite the believer quietly fighting temptation. Invite the seeker with questions. Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody behind a screen may be staring at a wall tonight.
Somebody is ashamed.
Somebody is thinking they have gone too far.
Somebody believes Jesus would never want them after what they did.
Somebody has been walking around the same Jericho for years.
Maybe your share becomes the moment they hear:
“Rahab had a past too.”
Maybe they read far enough to hear:
“Christ receives repentant sinners.”
Maybe they open a Bible.
Maybe they pray.
Maybe they come home.
But before you leave, look once more at Jericho.
A sealed city.
An impossible wall.
A strange command.
Days of obedience with no visible result.
Then the trumpet.
The shout.
The collapse.
And walking out from the ruins…
Rahab.
The woman whose past should have made her forgettable became a woman Scripture refused to forget.
Eventually her name would appear in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
That may be the detail your heart needed most.
Because perhaps you have spent years staring at the ruins and assuming ruins are all God can see.
But Jesus sees the repentant sinner who can be redeemed.
You see scandal.
Grace sees a place where redemption can write another ending.
You see the wall.
God sees beyond it.
You see what you were.
Christ calls His people toward what His grace is making them.
So keep walking when obedience feels quiet.
Keep trusting when you cannot see movement.
Keep repenting when pride tells you to hide.
Keep coming to Jesus when shame tells you to run.
And never mistake the silence before the wall falls for the absence of God.
Because one day you may discover that the wall you thought marked the end of your story was standing at the beginning of a testimony.
Jericho remembers the wall that fell. Heaven’s story remembers the woman grace brought out of the ruins.
